# 3.2 Batch Document Ingestion (insertMany())

> "insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...]) inserts multiple documents into a collection in a single call, passed as an array."

## 1. Operational Overview & Execution Context

To ingest multiple documents efficiently without incurring per-document network roundtrip overhead, MongoDB provides `db.<collectionName>.insertMany([<doc1>, <doc2>, ...])`. Passing an array of document objects persists the entire batch in a single call and returns a map of all generated `insertedIds`.

The diagram above demonstrates how `insertMany()` bundles an array of heterogeneous BSON documents into one batched write operation, assigning a distinct `ObjectId` to each element.

Within the broader parent module (**3. Document Ingestion Mechanics (CRUD Create)**), sub-topic `3.2` governs day-to-day developer workflows, driver execution behavior, and return telemetry.

## 2. Detailed Sub-Mechanism & Parameter Analysis

### 2.1 Command Syntax & Mandatory Array Wrapper (`[...]`) 

`insertMany()` strictly requires a JavaScript array (`[ { ... }, { ... } ]`) as its first parameter. Passing a single object without `[...]` throws a `MongoInvalidArgumentError`.

### 2.2 Single-Call Batching, Schema Flexibility & Return Payload

All documents in the array are transmitted in one network call. Because MongoDB is schema-flexible, documents inside the same `insertMany()` batch can have different fields. The method returns `{ acknowledged: true, insertedIds: { '0': ObjectId(...), '1': ObjectId(...) } }`.

## 3. Production `mongosh` Workflows & Return Telemetry

The following `mongosh` implementation demonstrates practical operational patterns, parameter combinations, and server acknowledgment telemetry for this sub-topic.

```javascript
// Batch insert multiple documents (notice heterogeneous fields in element 2)
db.students.insertMany([
  { name: "Meera", age: 17, grade: 7 },
  { name: "Kabir", age: 18, grade: 8, sports: ["Cricket"] }
]);
// Return Payload:
// {
//   acknowledged: true,
//   insertedIds: {
//     '0': ObjectId("6544b200c9e77c0012a40002"),
//     '1': ObjectId("6544b200c9e77c0012a40003")
//   }
// }
```

Always inspect the acknowledgment object or return payload emitted by `mongosh` to confirm that your operation matched and affected the expected namespace or document set.

## 4. Operational Execution Pipeline Diagram

The architectural flowchart below traces the decision branches, parameter validations, and execution outcomes across the L-2 and L-3 mindmap nodes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["db.students.insertMany([ d1, d2 ])"] --> B["Validates Array Wrapper [...]"]
    B --> C["Assigns Unique ObjectId to Each Element"]
    C --> D["Single Batched Network Write"]
    D --> E["Returns { acknowledged: true, insertedIds }"]
```

Understanding these operational branches prevents common runtime bugs during application development and database administration.

## 5. Multi-Dimension Comparison Matrix & Developer Pitfalls

| Comparison Dimension | `insertOne(doc)` | `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Parameter Type | Single Object `{ ... }` | Array of Objects `[ { ... }, { ... } ]` |
| Network Efficiency | `N` calls for `N` documents | `1` batched call for `N` documents |
| Schema Requirement | Flexible | Heterogeneous schemas allowed in same array |
| Return Telemetry | `{ acknowledged, insertedId }` | `{ acknowledged, insertedIds: { '0': ..., '1': ... } }` |

### Key Exam Traps & Takeaways

- **Exam Trap — Missing Array Brackets**: Calling `db.students.insertMany({ name: 'Meera' }, { name: 'Kabir' })` without `[...]` fails because the second argument is interpreted as the `options` object, not a document!
- **Auto-Creation on Batch Insert**: Just like `insertOne()`, calling `insertMany()` on a non-existent collection creates the collection automatically.
- **Indexed Map Return**: `insertedIds` is returned as an index-keyed object (`{ '0': ObjectId(...), '1': ObjectId(...) }`).
